newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Weakening Albanian lek seen partly a correction.
newsitem.headline: Weakening Albanian lek seen partly a correction.

text.p: The Albanian currency, the lek, has depreciated sharply against the dollar this year due to the collapse of pyramid savings schemes but the fall is partly seen by economists as an overdue correction.
The weakening lek has made life even tougher for Europe's poorest citizens, sending food prices soaring and inflation spiralling. Economists said this could weaken the lek further.

The Institute of Statistics said on Friday the Consumer Price Index in April fell 1.5 percent from March when it jumped 14 percent while year-on-year inflation was over 31 percent. Annual inflation in 1996 was 17.4 percent and six percent in 1995.
Since the start of 1997, the lek has weakened to between 148-152 leks to the dollar from about 100 in early January.
"The currency to a large extent reflects the inflationary trends," said Carlos Elbirt, the World Bank's resident representative in Albania.
"When the crisis erupted, the supply of goods stopped and prices rose. Some prices are now starting to come down again and the lek is remaining relatively stable."
The Central Bank said it intervened in the market on a couple of days in February but has not intervened since.
Most of the lek's fall was in January and February when the pyramid schemes collapsed, triggering widespread rioting and violence across the small Balkan country.
The lek had been relatively stable to the U.S. dollar, hovering at around 100 leks over the past three years.
However economists said the lek was considered overvalued in the second half of 1996, not reacting to deteriorating macroeconomic conditions in Albania.

With two of the most popular pyramid funds, Xhaferri and Populli, only accepting deposits in leks, Albanians receiving money from relatives working overseas had converted foreign currency into leks, propping up the unit.
Banking officials say $350-450 million was sent to Albania last year by its army of workers living and working abroad.
"This was a very important factor supporting the strength of the lek," said one financial analyst in Tirana.
The currency hit a two year high last November when the dollar traded down to 95 leks compared to 117 in early 1996.
"When the schemes collapsed in January the support for the lek was removed and we saw a correction."
The unit had not reacted to a growing budget deficit that expanded due to government spending in the run-up to a general election in May 1996 and local government elections in October.
The budget deficit amounted to 11 percent of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of $2.3 billion in 1996 against seven percent in 1995. It was expected to hit 15 percent this year.

"As long as the budget deficit and other elements are not under control, the underlying inflationary pressure is there and will be maintained and sooner or later the exchange rate will weaken further," Elbirt said.
The lek weakened slightly in early 1996 but recovered its strength due largely to the pyramids.
The central bank attributed the early 1996 weakening to high expenditure as newly privatised companies bought new equipment.
Other economists said the lek weakened in early 1996 after the end of a U.N. imposed oil embargo on Serbia and Montenegro.

"During the Yugoslav conflict an illicit and highly lucrative fuel trade developed between Albania and Montenegro and the smuggling brought a steady stream of hard currency into Albania," an Economist Intelligence Unit report said.
"Since the embargo ended the currency fell."
